title: Safe Type Checking
summary: Modern Java pattern matching for instanceof and clean type assertions.

activities.title: Practical Context: Modern Pattern Matching in Enterprise Java
activities.concept: Pattern Matching for instanceof (Identification + Binding in One Atomic Step)

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: In older phones, unlocking required two distinct steps: 1) You pressed the power button to wake the screen (type check), and then 2) You typed in a 6-digit PIN code to actually access your apps (casting). In modern smartphones with Face ID or fingerprint sensors, you look at the phone: it identifies you AND grants access immediately in one seamless, atomic motion.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: In legacy Java, type checking required two steps: `if (obj instanceof String)` followed by `String s = (String) obj;`. In modern Java (Java 16+), Pattern Matching for `instanceof` combines testing and extraction into a single atomic expression: `if (obj instanceof String s) { ... }`. The variable `s` is automatically typed, safely bound, and in scope.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: Pattern matching for instanceof combines type verification and variable binding, eliminating redundant and error-prone casts.

activities.content:
For decades, Java developers wrote boilerplate code checking `instanceof` followed immediately by an explicit cast on the next line.

This repetitive idiom was verbose and introduced subtle errors if the cast target differed from the type checked.

Modern Java introduced Pattern Matching for `instanceof`, streamlining type checks and variable binding into a single expressive statement.

activities.title: Safe Type Checking: Definition and Pattern Matching for instanceof
Legacy Cast vs Modern Pattern Matching
activities.explanation: Demonstrates modern pattern matching for instanceof. Pattern variables 's' and 'num' are automatically bound and usable in subsequent conditions with &&.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `printLegacy` requires checking `instanceof` and then explicitly casting `(String) obj`.
`printModern` uses `obj instanceof String s` to test and bind `s` in one step.
The compound condition `&& !s.isBlank()` safely accesses methods on `s` because `&&` short-circuits.
The `else if` demonstrates pattern matching with `Integer num`.

activities.title: Clean equals() Implementation with Pattern Matching
activities.explanation: Pattern matching streamlines equals() by removing the ugly manual cast. If obj is null or a different type, instanceof evaluates to false safely.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `if (this == obj) return true;` quickly handles reference identity.
`if (obj instanceof UserProfile other)` checks null, validates type, and casts to `other` simultaneously.

questions.question: Which Java version finalized Pattern Matching for instanceof as a standard language feature?
options: Java 8
Java 11
Java 16
Java 21
questions.explanation: Pattern Matching for instanceof was introduced as a preview in Java 14 and finalized as a permanent standard feature in Java 16 (JEP 394).

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of writing `if (obj instanceof String s)`?
options: It makes the JVM execute bytecode without CPU registers
It combines the type check and the cast into an atomic, error-proof operation
It automatically internizes all Strings
It turns String into a mutable buffer
questions.explanation: It eliminates the boilerplate manual cast `String s = (String) obj;` and avoids ClassCastException.

questions.question: What scoping rule does a pattern variable follow?
options: Lexical block scoping (always bounded by curly braces)
Flow scoping (in scope wherever the compiler can prove the pattern matched)
Global scope across the entire class
Package-private scope
questions.explanation: Pattern variables use flow scoping: they are in scope only in regions of code where the condition was evaluated as true.

questions.question: Which operator is legal to combine with pattern matching in the same if statement?
options: `&&` (logical AND)
`||` (logical OR)
`^` (bitwise XOR)
`~` (bitwise NOT)
questions.explanation: `&&` is legal because if the left pattern matches, the variable is guaranteed to be bound for the right expression. `||` is illegal because the right side could execute without the left matching.

questions.question: In the code: `if (!(obj instanceof String s)) return; System.out.println(s.length());`, why is `s` accessible after the if block?
options: It is a compiler bug in modern Java
Because of flow scoping: if execution proceeds past the if statement, the object MUST have been a String
Because return resets all local variables
Because String is final
questions.explanation: Flow scoping recognizes that if the method didn't return, `!(obj instanceof String s)` was false, meaning `obj` is definitely a String.

questions.question: What happens if `obj` is null in `if (obj instanceof String s)`?
options: NullPointerException is thrown
The if condition evaluates to false, and s is not bound
s is assigned the literal string 'null'
The JVM halts
questions.explanation: `instanceof` on null always evaluates to false, so the block is bypassed safely without NPE.

questions.question: Can a pattern variable have the same name as an existing local variable in the same scope?
options: Yes, it shadows the existing variable
No, declaring a pattern variable with the same name as an active local variable causes a compile error
Only if the existing variable is null
Only if the pattern variable is final
questions.explanation: Java forbids shadowing local variables with pattern variables in overlapping scopes to prevent ambiguity.

questions.question: Can pattern variables be modified (reassigned) inside the block?
options: No, pattern variables are implicitly final and cannot be modified
Yes, pattern variables are effectively final but can be reassigned unless declared with `final`
Only inside while loops
Only if passed to a setter
questions.explanation: Pattern variables are not implicitly final; you can reassign them unless you explicitly declare `final`: `if (obj instanceof final String s)`.

questions.question: How does pattern matching improve the readability of `equals(Object o)`?
options: It speeds up bytecode by 50%
It combines null check, class check, and casting into a single readable line `if (o instanceof MyClass other)`
It eliminates the need for hashCode()
It allows comparing private fields without getters
questions.explanation: It condenses three verbose steps (null check, type check, cast) into one clean check.

questions.question: Which statement is ILLEGAL in Java 16+?
options: `if (obj instanceof String s && s.length() > 0)`
`if (obj instanceof String s || s.length() > 0)`
`if (!(obj instanceof String s)) throw new IllegalArgumentException();`
`if (obj instanceof final String s)`
questions.explanation: Using `||` is illegal because if `obj` is not a String, `s` would be unbound when evaluating `s.length() > 0`.

interviewQA.question: What is Flow Scoping in the context of Java pattern matching?
interviewQA.answer: Flow scoping means that the scope of a pattern variable is determined by the flow of control, rather than syntactic curly-brace boundaries. A pattern variable is only in scope where the compiler can deduce that the pattern has definitely matched. For instance, in `if (obj instanceof String s && s.length() > 0)`, `s` is in scope on the right side of `&&`. But in `if (obj instanceof String s || ...) `, it is illegal because the right side executes when the match fails.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Flow scoping makes pattern variables visible only in execution paths where the pattern is guaranteed to have matched.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Flow scoping binds pattern variables strictly where match truth is guaranteed.
keyPoints: Flow scoping binds pattern variables strictly where match truth is guaranteed.

interviewQA.question: Why does the compiler forbid the `||` operator with pattern matching?
interviewQA.answer: The short-circuiting OR operator `||` evaluates its right-hand operand only when its left-hand operand evaluates to `false`. If the left operand `obj instanceof String s` is `false`, `s` has NOT been bound. Therefore, referring to `s` on the right side would access an unassigned variable. To guarantee type safety, the language specification forbids `||` when the pattern variable is referenced.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Because || evaluates the right side only when the left test fails, meaning the pattern variable is unbound.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Logical OR is forbidden with pattern variables due to unbound execution paths.
keyPoints: Logical OR is forbidden with pattern variables due to unbound execution paths.

interviewQA.question: Can pattern matching for `instanceof` be used with `final` modifiers?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. You can declare `if (obj instanceof final String s)`. This makes the pattern variable `s` explicitly `final`, preventing any reassignment to `s` within the body of the matching block.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes, pattern variables can be declared with final to enforce immutability within the block.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Pattern variables can be declared final explicitly.
keyPoints: Pattern variables can be declared final explicitly.

interviewQA.question: How did Pattern Matching for `instanceof` pave the way for Pattern Matching in `switch` statements (Java 21)?
interviewQA.answer: Pattern matching for `instanceof` was the foundational stepping stone in Project Amber. By standardizing type patterns and flow scoping, Java was able to expand pattern matching to `switch` expressions (JEP 441 in Java 21) and record deconstruction patterns (JEP 440), enabling powerful algebraic data types and pattern matching.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: It established pattern syntax and flow scoping rules that enabled switch pattern matching and record deconstruction.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Instanceof pattern matching laid the groundwork for modern Java switch expressions.
keyPoints: Instanceof pattern matching laid the groundwork for modern Java switch expressions.

interviewQA.question: How does early return interact with flow scoping?
interviewQA.answer: When an `if` block with a negated pattern exits the method (via `return`, `throw`, or infinite loop), the pattern variable remains in scope for the remainder of the enclosing method. For example: `if (!(obj instanceof User u)) return; System.out.println(u.getName());`. Because the method terminates if `obj` is not a `User`, any subsequent statement is guaranteed to execute only when `obj` is a `User`.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Negating the pattern and returning early extends the pattern variable's scope to the rest of the method.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Early exit guards extend pattern variable scope to subsequent method lines.
keyPoints: Early exit guards extend pattern variable scope to subsequent method lines.

interviewQA.question: Are pattern matching `instanceof` checks faster than traditional casting in bytecode?
interviewQA.answer: In bytecode, modern pattern matching still generates `instanceof` followed by `checkcast` and store instructions. The performance is practically identical. However, the elimination of human error, avoidance of accidental mismatched casts, and improved compiler optimization visibility make it strictly superior.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Bytecode execution is virtually identical, but code reliability and maintainability are vastly improved.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Pattern matching improves code quality without sacrificing performance.
keyPoints: Pattern matching improves code quality without sacrificing performance.

practiceProblems.title: Warmup: Modern Pattern Matching Formatter
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Refactor the legacy type formatter using Java 16+ pattern matching:
1. In `formatObject(Object obj)`:
   - If `obj instanceof String s`, return `'String: ' + s.toUpperCase()`
   - If `obj instanceof Integer i`, return `'Int: ' + (i * 10)`
   - Otherwise return `'Unknown'`
2. In `main`, call `formatObject` with `"java"`, `5`, and `3.14`.
Verify the output matches the expected strings without any manual casts.
hints: Use `if (obj instanceof String s)` and `else if (obj instanceof Integer i)`.
Access `s` and `i` directly without writing `(String) obj` or `(Integer) obj`.

practiceProblems.title: Compound Pattern Matching Validator
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a compound pattern matching validator from scratch without starter code:
1. Class `Validator` with static method `public static void validateInput(Object input)`:
   - If `input instanceof String s && s.length() >= 5`, print `'Valid long string: ' + s`
   - If `input instanceof String s && s.length() < 5`, print `'Short string rejected: ' + s`
   - If `input instanceof Double d && d > 0.0`, print `'Positive double: ' + d`
   - Otherwise, print `'Unsupported input'`
2. In `Main`, test `validateInput` with `"Administrator"`, `"Cat"`, `99.5`, and `-4.2`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Valid long string: Administrator
Short string rejected: Cat
Positive double: 99.5
Unsupported input
hints: Use compound `&&` in the if conditions to inspect length or numerical positivity.
-4.2 is not > 0.0, so it falls to 'Unsupported input'.

practiceProblems.title: Early Return Guard Clause Processor
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Implement an early return guard pattern from scratch without starter code:
1. Class `SecureMessage` with fields `sender` (String) and `content` (String). Constructor sets both. Methods `getSender()` and `getContent()`.
2. Class `MessageProcessor` with static method `public static void process(Object raw)`:
   - Guard clause: `if (!(raw instanceof SecureMessage msg)) { System.out.println("Error: Not a secure message"); return; }`
   - Because of flow scoping, `msg` is in scope below the guard! Print `'Processing message from ' + msg.getSender() + ': ' + msg.getContent()`.
3. In `Main`, call `process` with `new SecureMessage("Alice", "Top secret payload")` and with `"Just a plain string"`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Processing message from Alice: Top secret payload
Error: Not a secure message
hints: Use the early return guard: `if (!(raw instanceof SecureMessage msg)) return;`
Flow scoping automatically makes `msg` available in subsequent statements.

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Illegal OR Operator in Pattern Matching
practiceProblems.problemStatement: A developer tried to write a pattern matching check using `||` in `checkToken(Object obj)`, causing a compile-time error. Fix the code so it properly checks if `obj` is either a valid non-empty `String` or a positive `Integer`, printing `'Valid token'` or `'Invalid token'` accordingly.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Valid token: AUTH-XYZ
Invalid token
Valid token: 100
hints: Separate the conditions using `else if (obj instanceof Integer i && i > 0)` instead of trying to merge into a single illegal `||` expression.
Print 'Valid token: ' + i for positive integers.

practiceProblems.title: Advanced: Pattern Matching Domain Evaluator
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a domain expression evaluator from scratch without starter code:
1. Interface `Expr`
2. Class `Literal implements Expr`: field `value` (double). Method `getValue()`.
3. Class `Add implements Expr`: fields `left` (Expr) and `right` (Expr). Methods `getLeft()`, `getRight()`.
4. Class `Multiply implements Expr`: fields `left` (Expr) and `right` (Expr). Methods `getLeft()`, `getRight()`.
5. Class `Evaluator` with static method `public static double evaluate(Expr expr)` using recursive pattern matching:
   - `if (expr instanceof Literal lit) return lit.getValue();`
   - `if (expr instanceof Add add) return evaluate(add.getLeft()) + evaluate(add.getRight());`
   - `if (expr instanceof Multiply mul) return evaluate(mul.getLeft()) * evaluate(mul.getRight());`
   - Otherwise throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown expr")
6. In `Main`, construct `(3.0 + 4.0) * 2.0`:
   `Expr expr = new Multiply(new Add(new Literal(3.0), new Literal(4.0)), new Literal(2.0));`
7. Evaluate and print `'Result: ' + Evaluator.evaluate(expr)` (should output `'Result: 14.0'`).
hints: Recursively call evaluate() on the sub-expressions inside Add and Multiply.
